title: Graph Random Features for Scalable Gaussian Processes
one_liner: Use random walks to estimate graph similarities quickly, making Bayesian prediction on million-node graphs practical on a single computer.
lead: Gaussian processes (a tool for making principled guesses about unknown values) work perfectly on small graphs but become impossibly slow on large ones: they need to compute a similarity score between every pair of nodes, a task that takes hours even for modest sizes. This paper replaces the exact similarity table with a fast approximate one built from random walks, shrinking the slowest step from hours to minutes.

problem.h2: Exact similarity scores take forever on large graphs
paras: A Gaussian process (a statistical model that makes predictions with honest confidence intervals) works by comparing every pair of nodes on a graph. A node is similar to nodes it connects to, dissimilar to distant ones; the model captures this by building a similarity table: a grid where row i, column j tells how much node i resembles node j. Computing and storing this table, plus inverting it to make predictions, takes time proportional to the number of nodes cubed. On a million-node graph, that is a quintillion operations. Not practical.

A beginner might try: just use the raw edge list. But a Gaussian process needs a learned measure of similarity that accounts for the graph structure, not just direct edges. Using the edge list directly gives bad predictions.

callout.html: Instead of building an exact similarity table, estimate it using random walks, cutting the time from proportional to N cubed down to proportional to N to the one-point-five power.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: We want to learn on a huge graph but computing similarities between all node pairs takes N-cubed time.

panels.title: 2. Exact method is slow
panels.caption: Building the full similarity table is the slowest step; storing it needs gigabytes of memory.

panels.title: 3. Random walks sketch it
panels.viz_args: Random walkers hop around the graph
panels.caption: Launch random walkers that jump to neighboring nodes. Each walker traces a path through the graph.

panels.title: 4. Walkers estimate similarity
panels.caption: Paths that cross often come from similar regions; rare crossings mean distant nodes. Count crossings to estimate similarity.

panels.title: 5. Speed wins
panels.caption: Random-walk estimates run in sub-quadratic time and fit on a laptop, unlocking Bayesian optimization on a million nodes.

steps.b: 1. Take a graph and observed measurements
steps.text: You have a graph with millions of nodes and noisy observations (measurements) at some of those nodes.
Instead of computing exact node similarities, run many random walkers that hop to neighboring nodes and record their paths.
Paths that overlap frequently come from similar node neighborhoods. Paths that rarely meet come from distant regions. Count overlaps to estimate the similarity table.
Feed the estimated table into a solver that works without ever storing the full table explicitly, keeping memory low.

steps.b: 5. Make predictions and decide where to observe next
steps.text: Use the learned model to predict at all unobserved nodes and intelligently pick new nodes to measure, balancing exploration and reducing prediction uncertainty.

paras: The paper replaces an exact, slow similarity table with an approximate, fast one built from random walks. That single change makes Bayesian prediction on huge graphs tractable.

hidden.name: Walk overlap count
paras: Random walks are finite sequences of nodes visited by a walker hopping randomly. If two nodes are in similar neighborhoods, walks starting from them overlap more often. The hidden quantity the paper measures is: how many times do random paths cross? The more overlaps, the more similar the nodes.

The paper estimates this by sampling thousands of random walks, recording which nodes each walk visits, and counting overlaps between walks starting at different nodes. This overlap count, scaled correctly, is the random-walk estimator of the true similarity table.

heat.caption: Darker means more walk overlaps between two nodes; marked pairs are high-similarity node pairs.

reads.html: Imagine two nodes on the graph. If you launch random walkers at both nodes, do their paths cross often or rarely? More crossings mean the nodes are in similar neighborhoods.

The paper proves that the inner product of random feature vectors (computed from walk paths) concentrates around the true similarity value, enabling probabilistic accuracy guarantees even with finite samples.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: sampling beats exact computation
paras: The core reason this is faster: a Gaussian process needs to know similarity between nodes to make predictions because the strength of its confidence in a guess depends on how close the new node is to nodes it has already seen measurements from. Exact similarity requires computing a full table (time proportional to nodes cubed). Random walks give you a sparse, approximate version. Here is why the approximation is good enough.

Random walks naturally explore a graph according to its structure: nodes in dense clusters get revisited often, isolated nodes rarely. If you launch many random walks and record which nodes each one visits, walks starting near each other will share many nodes. Counting these shared nodes (weighted by how often they appear) estimates the true similarity. The paper proves (with probability bounds) that this estimate is close to the true value. Since a random walk samples only a tiny fraction of all possible paths, it is vastly faster.

The second speedup: you never explicitly form the similarity table. Instead, you use an iterative solver that multiplies by the table implicitly, using the walks on the fly. This cuts memory from quadratic (storage for the full table) to linear in the number of walks, which is independent of the graph size. On a million-node graph, this means using a laptop instead of a data center.

stages.s: Graph with N nodes and noisy measurements at some nodes
Sample random walks from each node
Count walk overlaps to estimate node similarities
Use an iterative solver with implicit table multiplies
Predictions and uncertainty at all nodes, in sub-quadratic time

math.words: The random walk estimate Phi approximates the true kernel K by averaging random feature vectors. Each random feature vector for node i is built by sampling a walk starting at i, recording which nodes it visits, and weighting them by the walk probabilities. The estimated kernel at node pair (i,j) is the inner product of their random feature vectors.
math.equation: Estimated kernel K-hat[i,j] = Phi[i] dot Phi[j], where Phi[i] is built from random walks starting at node i
symbols: random feature vector for node i, built from its walks
inner product of the two feature vectors = estimated similarity
the true similarity matrix (expensive to compute exactly)
number of random walks sampled to estimate the features
the approximation error threshold in the probability bound

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say node 1 and node 2 are close in a graph. We launch 100 random walks starting at node 1 and 100 starting at node 2.
Walks from node 1 visit: {1,3,5} 80 times, {1,4} 20 times.
Walks from node 2 visit: {2,3,5} 75 times, {2,4,6} 25 times.
Common neighborhood {3,5} appears in 80 walks from node 1 and 75 walks from node 2 -> high overlap.
We weight these overlaps and compute their inner product -> estimate of K[1,2] ≈ 0.78 (close to true value).
Same process for all pairs, but using only O(n) walks per node, not checking all N pairs explicitly.

math.note: The random walk estimator is an unbiased Monte Carlo approximation: on average, the walk-based inner product equals the true similarity, and more walks reduce the variance.

bars.h2: Scaling trade-off: exact vs. random walks

charts.title: Exact Gaussian process
charts.note: Exact method is accurate but extremely slow and memory-hungry on large graphs.

charts.title: Graph random features
charts.note: Random-walk version scales to million-node graphs on a laptop while keeping predictions accurate.

items.b: Too few random walks: variance in the estimator.
items.html: If you launch only a handful of walks per node, the random-walk similarities have high variance (they bounce around) because overlap counts from small samples are unreliable. The paper provides a formula for how many walks you need; fewer walks are faster but less stable because averaging over more independent samples reduces randomness.

Random walks assume the graph is connected and well-mixed. On graphs with isolated clusters, walks rarely cross between clusters, so cross-cluster similarities are estimated poorly. The method works best on well-mixed graphs.

Random walks have tuning parameters: walk length, termination probability, number of walks. Choosing them requires pilot experiments. Too-short walks underestimate long-range similarity; too-long walks waste computation.

Use the probabilistic accuracy guarantees in the paper to choose the number of walks for your target error. On graphs with clustering, apply the method per-cluster first. The payoff: run Bayesian optimization on graphs 1000x larger than before.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic graph (e.g., a random regular graph or a real social network with 50,000 nodes). Observe noisy measurements at a small random subset of nodes (e.g., 100 nodes). Use the graph random features method to make predictions at all unobserved nodes. Compare wall-clock time and memory to a baseline (e.g., random search or an approximate similarity baseline). Track prediction error on a held-out test set of measured nodes.
demo.metric_eq: Speedup = time_exact / time_GRF. Memory ratio = memory_exact / memory_GRF. Prediction accuracy = test accuracy of GRF vs exact Gaussian process.
demo.closing: The demo must show that on large graphs, GRFs run 10-100x faster and use 10x less memory while achieving similar or better prediction accuracy compared to exact methods or naive baselines, because sub-quadratic time and linear memory allow you to scale to graphs that exact methods cannot handle at all.
